title: Today and open questions
text:
15_03  TODAY AND OPEN QUESTIONS

We began this book with a scribe in ancient Egypt describing head injuries on papyrus, and with Greek physicians arguing over whether thought lived in the heart or the brain. We end in a period when neuroscientists can switch on genetically chosen neurons with light, record from tens of thousands of cells at once, map every synapse in a fly's brain, and let a paralysed person speak through a computer. It would be easy to conclude that the brain is nearly understood. It is not. This last section takes stock of where neuroscience stands as of the mid-2020s, which large projects shape it, and which questions remain open, with an eye on those where AI is likely to matter most.

THE SHAPE OF THE FIELD TODAY

Neuroscience is now a large, interdisciplinary enterprise with several distinctive features.

Big projects and consortia. The US BRAIN Initiative (Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies), announced in 2013 and run substantially through the National Institutes of Health, has funded tool development, cell-type census efforts, and large-scale recording. A major product is the BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network and its successor projects, which used single-cell RNA sequencing and other methods to classify cell types; a collection of papers published in 2023 described a cell-type atlas of the whole mouse brain with thousands of transcriptomically defined cell types, along with extensive surveys of human brain cells. The European Human Brain Project ran from 2013 to 2023 and produced the EBRAINS research infrastructure for data and simulation. National programmes in other countries, including Japan, China, Korea and Australia, have their own brain initiatives. The Allen Institute releases large open datasets, from gene expression atlases to the Brain Observatory and MICrONS connectome (Chapter 12).

Open data and open tools. Standards such as Neurodata Without Borders for physiology and BIDS for imaging, archives such as DANDI and OpenNeuro, and open-source tools like Suite2p, Kilosort and DeepLabCut mean that much analysis can now be done by people who did not collect the data. This lowers the barrier for computationally trained students, including those from engineering backgrounds.

Massive recording and perturbation. Neuropixels probes (Chapter 10) record from thousands of sites across many brain regions; the International Brain Laboratory, a consortium of laboratories, used standardised procedures to record across much of the mouse brain during a single decision task, publishing a brain-wide map in 2025. Combined with optogenetics and imaging, these tools allow experiments that tie behaviour, populations and cell types together.

Theory and AI. Computational and theoretical neuroscience, once a small subfield, is now central, and machine learning is part of almost every experimental pipeline.

OPEN QUESTION 1: HOW DOES THE BRAIN LEARN?

Despite Hebb, LTP, STDP, dopamine and decades of theory (Chapters 6 and 7), we do not know the learning algorithm of the cortex. Does it approximate gradient descent, and if so how is credit assigned across many layers and long time delays? Candidate mechanisms include three-factor rules with neuromodulators, dendritic compartments that carry error signals separately from feedforward input, predictive coding, and learning driven by replay during sleep. Testing them requires measuring synaptic changes in identified neurons during learning in behaving animals, which is becoming possible with imaging of dendritic spines and voltage indicators, but remains hard. For AI, an answer could suggest learning rules that are local, online and energy efficient.

OPEN QUESTION 2: HOW ARE MEMORIES STORED AND RETRIEVED OVER A LIFETIME?

Chapter 9 described engram cells, hippocampal replay and systems consolidation. But the physical basis of very long-term memory, lasting decades despite constant protein turnover at synapses, is not fully understood; proposals include persistent molecular switches, structural changes and redundant distributed storage. How memories are reorganised over time, how they avoid interfering with each other, and why they fail in diseases such as Alzheimer's are central questions. The World Health Organization estimates that tens of millions of people worldwide live with dementia. Machine learning faces the same problems of storage, interference and retrieval, as Chapters 9 and 11 discussed, and solutions may inform each other.

OPEN QUESTION 3: WHAT IS THE ROLE OF THE WHOLE-BRAIN STATE?

Recordings revealing movement-related activity throughout cortex (Chapter 12), the large influence of arousal and neuromodulators, and brain-wide representations of task variables have moved the field away from strictly modular pictures. How do local circuits and global states interact? How do sleep and wakefulness, attention and arousal switch the brain between computational modes? AI systems lack anything like global neuromodulation of state, though some research explores analogous mechanisms.

OPEN QUESTION 4: HOW DO COGNITION AND LANGUAGE ARISE FROM CIRCUITS?

We know much about vision, movement, and simple decisions in animals, and much less about the circuit-level basis of abstract reasoning, planning, and language, which are hardest to study in animal models. Human recordings, from epilepsy patients with implanted electrodes and from BCI participants (Chapter 14), have become increasingly important. The surprising success of large language models has made questions about language in the brain more urgent: how similar are the brain's representations of language to those in language models, and what does the similarity mean? Researchers including Evelina Fedorenko have argued, from neuroimaging, that the human language network is distinct from networks supporting reasoning and other thought, which bears on whether language models' fluency implies reasoning.

OPEN QUESTION 5: CONSCIOUSNESS

Whether, how and why physical processes give rise to subjective experience remains among the hardest questions in science. Scientific theories of consciousness include global workspace theory (developed by Bernard Baars and, in neural form, by Stanislas Dehaene and colleagues), integrated information theory (developed by Giulio Tononi), higher-order theories, and recurrent processing theory. In 2023 results were published from an "adversarial collaboration", in which proponents of global neuronal workspace theory and integrated information theory agreed in advance on experiments whose outcomes might distinguish them; the results challenged some predictions of both theories, and the debate continued, including public disagreement about whether integrated information theory should be considered scientific. The question has become practical because of AI: whether artificial systems could be conscious, and how one would know, is now discussed by researchers in both fields, with a 2023 report by Patrick Butlin, Robert Long and colleagues assessing AI systems against indicator properties derived from neuroscientific theories, concluding that no current system was a strong candidate but that there were no obvious technical barriers to building systems satisfying the indicators. These are questions on which reasonable experts disagree, and readers should be skeptical of confident claims in either direction.

OPEN QUESTION 6: HOW TO TREAT BRAIN DISORDERS?

Despite advances in understanding, treatments for many psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders remain limited. Deep brain stimulation helps many people with Parkinson's disease; adaptive, closed-loop stimulation systems that adjust to recorded neural signals are now being tested and deployed. Antibody therapies targeting amyloid have shown modest slowing of decline in early Alzheimer's disease in clinical trials, alongside debate about the size of benefit and risks. Gene therapies, optogenetic vision restoration (12_01), and BCIs (Chapter 14) show what engineering approaches can do. Machine learning is being applied to diagnosis from imaging, EEG and speech, to predicting seizures, and to designing stimulation, with the usual caveats about validation and bias.

OPEN QUESTION 7: WHAT IS THE RIGHT LEVEL OF DESCRIPTION?

Running through the whole book is a question of level. Is the brain best understood as ion channels and cables (Chapter 5), as synapses and cell types (Chapters 6 and 12), as population dynamics (Chapter 13), as an optimiser of objectives (15_02), or as an inference engine (13_03)? The answer is surely "all of the above, at different scales", but how to connect the levels, how a change in a channel affects behaviour, remains a deep challenge. AI offers a cautionary parallel: we know every equation in a transformer, yet understanding how it performs a given computation requires dedicated interpretability research. Complete knowledge of the lowest level does not automatically give understanding at higher levels.

WHERE AI AND NEUROSCIENCE MAY GO TOGETHER

Some directions are already visible.

Foundation models of the brain. Researchers are training large models on neural recordings across many animals and sessions, aiming for general-purpose models that predict neural activity, decode behaviour and transfer to new subjects. "Digital twin" models of mouse visual cortex trained on large recordings have been used to design stimuli that drive particular neurons, with predictions tested back in the animal.

Closed-loop science. Automated experiments in which AI systems choose stimuli or perturbations to test hypotheses, then update models, could speed discovery.

Brain-inspired efficiency. As AI's energy and data demands grow, interest in sparse, event-driven and local-learning approaches is increasing, with neuromorphic hardware a candidate platform (13_04).

Shared theory. Ideas such as prediction, compression, representation geometry and credit assignment may form a common theoretical vocabulary for intelligence in brains and machines.

Neurotechnology. BCIs combining implants, deep learning and language models are moving from laboratories toward clinical products, raising the ethical issues in 14_03.

A NOTE TO THE READER

This book was written for a mechatronics student interested in AI, and it is worth ending with why that background is valuable. Neuroscience has always advanced through instruments: Galvani's frogs and conductors, Helmholtz's timing apparatus, the oscilloscopes of Adrian, the voltage clamp of Hodgkin and Huxley, the microelectrodes of Hubel and Wiesel, MRI scanners, optical fibres for optogenetics, two-photon microscopes, Neuropixels probes, and the implants of BCIs. Each was an engineering achievement. The field's mathematics, from the Nernst equation and cable theory to Kalman filters and gradient descent, is the mathematics of electrical engineering and control. And the field's current bottlenecks, recording more neurons with less damage, implants that last, low-power wireless electronics, real-time decoders, and closed-loop control, are engineering bottlenecks.

The ancient Egyptian surgeon wrote that certain head injuries were "an ailment not to be treated". Today many of those injuries are still beyond repair, but the list of things that can be measured, modelled and sometimes restored grows each decade, mostly because people combined biology with engineering and mathematics. That combination is exactly the one a student of mechatronics and AI is positioned to bring.

SUMMARY

As of the mid-2020s, neuroscience is a large, data-rich, tool-driven, open and computational field, shaped by projects such as the BRAIN Initiative, EBRAINS and the Allen Institute's open datasets. Major open questions include the brain's learning algorithm, lifelong memory, whole-brain state, the circuit basis of cognition and language, consciousness, treatment of disorders, and how to connect levels of description. AI is entangled with each, as model, tool and comparison, and the engineering skills that built neuroscience's instruments remain central to its future.
